chapter_summary:
Welcome to the final module of our Ethereum Developer Certification! As you progress from building functional DApps to deploying production-ready solutions, understanding and optimizing gas consumption becomes paramount. Gas is the unit of computational effort required to execute operations on the Ethereum network. Every transaction, from a simple Ether transfer to a complex smart contract interaction, consumes gas. This gas is paid in Ether to miners (or validators in Eth2) who process the transactions, ensuring the network's security and preventing spam. High gas costs can make your DApp prohibitively expensive to use, deterring adoption. Therefore, mastering gas optimization is not just a technical skill, but a crucial economic one for any serious Ethereum developer.

The cost of a transaction is calculated as `gasUsed * gasPrice`. While `gasPrice` is determined by network demand and user willingness to pay, `gasUsed` is directly influenced by the efficiency of your smart contract code. Our goal in this chapter is to minimize `gasUsed`. We'll explore various techniques, starting with fundamental Solidity principles and moving towards more advanced patterns. One of the first principles is to minimize state changes. Writing to storage (`sload` and `sstore` opcodes) is by far the most expensive operation. Reading from storage is also costly, though less so than writing. Conversely, operations involving memory or purely computational tasks are significantly cheaper. This distinction is critical: always prefer memory over storage when possible for temporary variables or function arguments. For instance, if you have an array that is only needed within a function's scope, declare it as `memory` rather than `storage`.

Consider data types and their packing. Solidity variables are stored in 256-bit slots. If you declare multiple smaller variables (e.g., `uint8`, `uint16`, `bool`) consecutively in a `struct` or as state variables, the Solidity compiler can pack them into a single storage slot, saving gas. For example, declaring `uint8 a; uint8 b; uint256 c;` will use two storage slots (a and b packed, c in its own slot), whereas `uint256 c; uint8 a; uint8 b;` will use three slots because `c` takes a full slot, preventing `a` and `b` from being packed with it. Always group smaller data types together. Similarly, avoid unnecessary `uint256` variables if a smaller type like `uint64` or `uint128` suffices, though the packing benefit is usually more significant.

Loops are another area ripe for optimization. While essential, unbounded loops that iterate over large data sets in storage can quickly exhaust the gas limit. If you must iterate, consider externalizing the iteration process (e.g., having users claim items one by one) or using pagination. When iterating over arrays, prefer `while` loops over `for` loops if the loop condition can be met more efficiently. Also, caching state variables in memory before a loop can save gas. Instead of `myArray[i].someProperty` inside a loop, load `myArray[i]` into a `memory` variable once per iteration and then access its properties. This avoids repeated storage reads.

Function visibility also plays a role. `external` functions are generally cheaper than `public` functions when dealing with arrays because `external` functions receive arguments directly from calldata, avoiding memory copying for arrays and structs. `public` functions, on the other hand, copy `calldata` arguments to `memory` by default. For internal helper functions, mark them `private` or `internal` to prevent external calls and potentially allow the compiler to optimize them further.

Short-circuiting logic in conditional statements (`&&`, `||`) can also save gas. If the first condition in an `&&` statement is false, the second condition is not evaluated. Similarly, if the first condition in an `||` statement is true, the second is skipped. Structure your conditions to put the cheapest or most likely-to-fail checks first. For example, `require(msg.sender == owner && amount > 0, "Invalid call");` is more gas-efficient if `msg.sender == owner` is often false, as it avoids evaluating `amount > 0`.

When making external calls, be mindful of the `gas` stipend. If you're calling another contract, explicitly specify the gas limit using `call{gas: 20000}(...)`. If not specified, all remaining gas is forwarded, which can be risky for reentrancy or simply wasteful if the called function doesn't need much gas. Be cautious with external calls in general, as they introduce external dependencies and potential reentrancy vulnerabilities, which we'll cover in a later chapter.

Finally, consider the use of `delete` and `emit` events. `delete`ing a storage variable (setting it to its zero value) actually *refunds* gas. This is an incentive mechanism to clear up "storage rent" on the blockchain. However, don't delete just for the refund; use it when state is truly no longer needed. `emit`ting events is relatively cheap as event data is stored in transaction logs, not on-chain state, making them excellent for off-chain indexing and UI updates without incurring high storage costs.

Measuring gas consumption is crucial for effective optimization. Tools like Hardhat's `hardhat-gas-reporter` or Remix's built-in gas profiler can help you analyze the gas cost of individual function calls and transactions. Always test your optimizations thoroughly to ensure they don't introduce bugs or unexpected behavior. Gas optimization is an iterative process, requiring careful analysis, implementation, and testing. By applying these techniques, you'll build more efficient, user-friendly, and cost-effective DApps.

screens.title: Gas Optimization Techniques
screens.subtitle: Write smarter contracts to reduce gasUsed and lower costs for your users

narration.text: In this lesson we will treat gas as both a technical and an economic constraint. Gas is the unit of computational effort used by Ethereum, and the cost of any transaction is the product of gasUsed and gasPrice. While gasPrice comes from the network and user choices, gasUsed is under your control as a developer. That means your Solidity choices directly affect how expensive your DApp is to use. We will focus on practical code-level strategies that lower gasUsed: preferring memory for temporary data, grouping small variables for storage packing, minimizing storage writes, caching values in loops, choosing function visibility wisely, using short-circuit logic, and handling external calls with explicit gas limits. You will also learn how to measure improvements with tools like Remix or Hardhat reporters and verify that your refactors actually save gas. By the end, you should be able to spot costly operations in a contract and apply changes that make real, measurable differences in transaction cost. Think about cost from the user's perspective — small savings per call compound quickly across many transactions. Which operation in your next contract will you optimize first?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Reduce gasUsed through storage-aware coding, better data layouts, and measured refactoring so your DApp is cheaper and more usable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus on measurable developer skills. First, you will understand what gas is in Ethereum and why gasUsed, not just gasPrice, is the part you can control through code. That understanding ties directly to the second objective: identifying which Solidity patterns are gas-intensive, such as storage writes and unbounded loops, and being able to measure gas consumption during development. Third, you will implement code-level strategies like using memory for temporary arrays, grouping small state variables for packing, caching values in loops, and choosing function visibility to reduce unnecessary copying. Lastly, you will apply best practices for storage management — including when to delete state and when to emit events for off-chain indexing — so your contract is both efficient and auditable. Each objective combines a concept, a measurable behavior, and a testable outcome so you can verify competency with gas reports or transaction traces. Think about an upcoming contract you might optimize using these objectives as checkpoints.

screens.subtitle: How you'll prove that optimizations work

narration.text: Optimization must be measurable. This screen expands on how you will practice the objectives and the supporting behaviors you should demonstrate. You will instrument contracts with gas profiling tools like Hardhat's gas reporter or Remix's gas profiler to record gasUsed for key functions before and after changes. In code, you will perform controlled refactors: replace repeated storage reads with cached memory variables, reorder state variables for packing, change public functions to external where arrays are passed in, and use delete when state is truly obsolete to capture refunds. Each practice step must be validated with a transaction trace or gas report. Misconceptions to avoid: micro-optimizations without measurement can add complexity with little benefit; deleting state for refunds is useful but should not be abused purely to game refunds. Approach each change as an experiment: hypothesis, change, measurement, and rollback if no benefit. Which function in your project will you measure first?

screens.title: What is Gas and Why It Matters
screens.subtitle: Understand gasUsed × gasPrice and its impact on users

narration.text: Gas is the unit of computational effort on Ethereum. Each operation executed by the EVM consumes gas; the total transaction cost is gasUsed multiplied by gasPrice. This matters because gasPrice fluctuates with network demand and user bidding, but gasUsed is determined by your smart contract code. Optimizing gasUsed directly reduces user fees and makes your DApp more accessible. For example, replacing an unnecessary storage write with a memory operation reduces gasUsed for that transaction. A common misconception is to focus only on gasPrice; while market conditions influence final cost, well-optimized contracts are cheaper across all price regimes. Another misconception is assuming that small savings are irrelevant; in applications with many users or frequent interactions, small per-call savings compound into significant cost differences. Consider a function that writes multiple variables: minimizing state writes or packing several small flags into a single slot can lower gasUsed substantially. The core takeaway is to treat gas as a first-class design constraint: when choosing a data layout or function visibility, ask how each decision changes gasUsed and whether it improves the user experience. What one change could you make now to reduce gasUsed in a routine transaction?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Gas quantifies EVM work; lower gasUsed means lower Ether cost for users and better adoption of your DApp.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Gas basics
Core definition

Gas is the unit of computational effort. Cost equals gasUsed times gasPrice. You control gasUsed through code design.

Example: Replacing a storage write with a memory variable for a temporary value reduces gasUsed.
Misconception: Optimizing only gasPrice creates no guarantees. GasUsed reduction benefits every user regardless of price.
Key Takeaway

Design contracts to minimize gasUsed; the network will handle gasPrice.

Supporting points
  • gasPrice is external; gasUsed is code-dependent.
  • Storage writes (sstore) are the most expensive operations.
  • Small per-call savings add up across many transactions.
Concrete scenario
A marketplace with thousands of sales per day benefits more from lower gasUsed per sale than from chasing low gasPrice windows.

screens.title: Storage vs. Memory
screens.subtitle: When to use storage, memory, and calldata

narration.text: Understanding storage and memory is one of the most practical gas optimizations you can learn. Storage variables persist on-chain and are expensive to read and write because they map to sload and sstore operations. Memory is ephemeral and far cheaper; it exists only for the transaction's execution. Calldata is an immutable, cheap area for external function parameters. The rule of thumb is: prefer memory for temporary arrays or variables that do not need to persist after the function returns. For example, if you build an array only to calculate a result within a function, declare it as memory instead of storage to avoid sstore and repeated sload costs. A common pitfall is using storage for local collections out of convenience; that quickly inflates gasUsed. Another concrete choice is function visibility: external functions receive arrays in calldata directly, avoiding an automatic copy into memory that public functions perform. If a function only needs to read an input array and is externally callable, prefer external and calldata to reduce copying. Finally, always measure: if a memory allocation still seems costly, test the gas profile. Which of your helper functions unnecessarily uses storage?

keyIdea.title: Memory rule
keyIdea.text: Use memory for temporary data and calldata for external array parameters to avoid unnecessary storage operations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Storage vs Memory
Comparison table
Storage

Persistent, expensive reads and writes (sload/sstore). Use for true state.

Memory

Temporary, cheaper. Use for in-function arrays and scratch data.

Calldata

Read-only external parameters. Avoids copying when used with external functions.

When to choose

If data need not persist, prefer memory or calldata to lower gasUsed.

Key Takeaway

Avoid storage for temporary data; choose calldata for externally passed arrays.

Supporting explanation
  • Storage operations are persistently recorded and therefore costly.
  • Memory allocations are per-transaction and far cheaper for temporary use.
  • External + calldata avoids copying arrays into memory, saving gas.
Concrete example
If you only need to sum an on-chain array within a view function, copy necessary fields into memory or accept the array via calldata in an external function to avoid repeated sloads.

screens.title: Data Packing and Variable Ordering
screens.subtitle: Group small variables to reduce storage slots

narration.text: Solidity stores state variables in 256-bit slots. If you declare several small variables consecutively, the compiler can pack them into a single slot and save storage writes and reads. For instance, two uint8 fields declared together can share one slot, while an intervening uint256 will force separate slots and defeat packing. This has a concrete gas impact: packing reduces the number of sstore/sload operations required to persist or read those fields. A frequent error is to default to uint256 for everything. While uint256 is convenient and sometimes necessary, smaller types like uint8 or uint128 are appropriate when the value range allows it. The practical rule is to group small types together and place larger types last. A misconception is that smaller types always lower gas; they only reduce storage cost when placed so the compiler can pack them. When designing structs or state layout, plan the order of fields deliberately. Before changing types, run tests and gas measurements to confirm the packing benefit in your particular contract. Data Packing and Variable Ordering means place multiple small-sized variables consecutively so the compiler can pack them into fewer 256-bit storage slots.. In practical terms, group small variables to reduce storage slots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Packing rule
keyIdea.text: Place multiple small-sized variables consecutively so the compiler can pack them into fewer 256-bit storage slots.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Data packing
Packing example
Poor order
uint256 c; uint8 a; uint8 b; — results in three storage slots because uint256 prevents packing.
Packed order
uint8 a; uint8 b; uint256 c; — a and b pack into one slot, c uses another slot, saving a slot versus the poor order.
Supporting notes
  • Group small types together to allow packing into 256-bit slots.
  • Switching types without reordering may not produce savings.
  • Always test gasUsed after changing types and layout.
Analogy
Think of packing like filling boxes: small items grouped together fill a single box instead of leaving wasted space next to large items.

screens.title: Optimizing Loops and Iteration
screens.subtitle: Avoid unbounded storage loops and cache state accesses

narration.text: Loops are conceptually simple but can become expensive on-chain, especially when iterating over storage. An unbounded loop that grows with dataset size can run into gas limits. First, avoid doing large iterations in a single transaction. If you must process many items, consider externalizing work — for example, let users claim items one by one or implement pagination so each transaction does a bounded amount of work. Second, cache storage reads before the loop. Accessing myArray[i]. someProperty repeatedly causes repeated sloads; instead, load myArray[i] into a memory variable once per iteration and read its fields from memory. This lowers gasUsed by removing repeated storage reads. Another practical tip is to cache the array length in a local variable instead of reading myArray. length every loop iteration if the length access would be expensive. A common misconception is that for and while loops have identical cost; sometimes a while loop can be structured more cheaply depending on the condition evaluation. Always reason about the maximum work the loop performs and measure gasUsed on representative data sizes. How might you redesign a function that currently iterates over an ever-growing array?

keyIdea.title: Loop rule
keyIdea.text: Keep per-transaction work bounded, cache storage reads into memory, and prefer user-driven or paginated processing for large data.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Loop optimization
Step-by-step refactor
  1. Identify unbounded loops over storage arrays.
  2. Consider externalizing work: let users claim or process items incrementally.
  3. Cache array length to a local variable once before the loop.
  4. Load each element into memory once per iteration and access fields from memory.
Concrete example
Instead of myArray[i].field inside the loop, do Struct memory item = myArray[i]; then use item.field to avoid repeated sloads.
Common mistakes
  • Leaving loops unbounded and assuming gas will always be sufficient.
  • Repeatedly reading from storage instead of caching into memory.
  • Using heavy computations inside loops without testing on realistic sizes.

screens.title: Function Visibility: public vs external
screens.subtitle: Choose visibility to avoid unnecessary copying

narration.text: Function visibility affects gas when working with arrays and structs. External functions receive calldata parameters directly, which avoids copying array data into memory. Public functions, by contrast, copy calldata arguments to memory, which can add gas overhead when passing large arrays. If a function is only intended to be called from outside the contract and takes arrays as inputs, prefer external to reduce gasUsed. For internal helper functions that are not part of the public A P I, mark them internal or private to help the compiler optimize and prevent external access. A misconception is that external is always cheaper; external is cheaper specifically when large calldata parameters would otherwise be copied. For functions without array parameters or with only single-value arguments, the difference may be negligible. Test both versions in your environment: deploy both and use a gas reporter to compare. Which signature in your code currently copies large calldata into memory unnecessarily? Function Visibility: public vs external means use external for functions that accept large calldata arrays from external callers; use internal/private for helpers to allow optimizations.. In practical terms, choose visibility to avoid unnecessary copying. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Visibility rule
keyIdea.text: Use external for functions that accept large calldata arrays from external callers; use internal/private for helpers to allow optimizations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Visibility choices
Public vs External
External functions accept calldata and avoid copying arrays into memory. Public functions copy calldata to memory, which costs gas when arrays are large.
Concrete example
If your contract has function process(uint256[] calldata items) external, it will avoid memory copying that a public counter-part would incur.
Supporting tips
  • Use external for array-heavy public API calls to reduce copies.
  • Mark internal helpers private/internal for compiler optimizations.
  • Measure gas to confirm the benefit for your call patterns.

screens.title: Short-circuiting Conditional Logic
screens.subtitle: Order checks to skip expensive evaluations

narration.text: Short-circuiting lets you save gas by structuring boolean expressions so cheap or likely-failing checks run first. In an && expression, if the first check is false, subsequent checks are not evaluated; in an || expression, if the first check is true, subsequent checks are skipped. Use this to avoid expensive computations or storage reads when an early, cheap test will fail or pass. For instance, placing a quick ownership check first can avoid more costly math or storage calls that would otherwise run. A misconception is that order never matters; in fact, evaluation order directly affects whether later expressions execute at all. Another concrete example is combining an on-chain flag check with a complex storage read. Put the flag check first if it frequently blocks execution. Short-circuiting is a small change with predictable gas savings when used where expensive evaluations can be avoided. When rewriting conditionals, test that logic equivalence is maintained and confirm gas differences with a profiler. Short-circuiting Conditional Logic means place cheap or likely-to-fail checks first so expensive evaluations are skipped whenever possible, saving gas.. In practical terms, order checks to skip expensive evaluations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Short-circuit rule
keyIdea.text: Place cheap or likely-to-fail checks first so expensive evaluations are skipped whenever possible, saving gas.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Short-circuiting
Pattern

Write conditionals so cheap checks or checks likely to be false come first to prevent expensive subsequent evaluations.

Example
Use require(msg.sender == owner && amount > 0) when owner check is often false, avoiding amount evaluation in that case.
Why it helps
  • Skips expensive code paths when earlier checks fail.
  • Reduces gasUsed by avoiding unnecessary evaluations.
  • Requires careful ordering to preserve logic and security.

screens.title: External Calls and Gas Stipend
screens.subtitle: Be explicit and cautious when calling other contracts

narration.text: External calls traverse contract boundaries and forward gas to the called contract. If you don't specify a gas limit, the call forwards all remaining gas which can be wasteful or introduce reentrancy risk. The chapter suggests using explicit gas limits such as call{gas: 20000} to restrict forwarded gas when the callee does not need much. Be mindful that external calls increase attack surface and can consume unpredictable gas depending on the callee's code path. A common misconception is to assume a callee will always behave benignly; defensive patterns and explicit gas limits reduce risk. Also, external calls can fail and bubble up exceptions, so handle return values and reverts carefully. In summary, only forward as much gas as the callee needs, and design call sequences to minimize external dependencies where possible. When you do make external calls, consider how gas and reentrancy interact and test those conditions thoroughly. External Calls and Gas Stipend means specify gas when making external calls and treat cross-contract calls as potential sources of extra gas and risk.. In practical terms, be explicit and cautious when calling other contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: External call rule
keyIdea.text: Specify gas when making external calls and treat cross-contract calls as potential sources of extra gas and risk.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › External calls
Practical guidance
  • Specify gas limits when calling other contracts to avoid forwarding unnecessary gas.
  • Treat external calls as potential reentrancy vectors and test carefully.
  • Handle return values and errors explicitly to avoid unexpected failures.
Concrete detail
Example: call{gas: 20000}(...) forwards a bounded amount of gas. Only forward what the callee needs and prefer minimal dependencies for critical state changes.
Pro Tip

If possible, perform critical state changes before external calls, then emit events rather than relying on external confirmations.

screens.title: delete and emit: Refunds and Logs
screens.subtitle: Use delete for gas refunds and events for off-chain data

narration.text: Deleting storage can generate gas refunds. When you set a storage slot back to its zero value with delete, the EVM refunds some gas as an incentive to reduce on-chain state. This mechanism encourages reclaiming storage that is no longer necessary. However, deleting solely to receive refunds is a mistake; use delete when state is truly no longer needed to avoid complicating contract logic. Emitted events are cheaper than storing the same data on-chain because event data is recorded in transaction logs, not in state, making events a great option for off-chain indexing and UI updates without incurring expensive sstore operations. A misconception is treating events as part of guaranteed on-chain state; they are not retrievable by on-chain logic and are intended for off-chain consumers. Use events to communicate information and state changes to UIs and relayers while keeping persistent state minimal. Balance refunds and event usage with clear semantics so your contract remains maintainable and predictable. delete and emit: Refunds and Logs means delete unused storage to earn refunds and emit events for off-chain needs rather than storing everything on-chain.. In practical terms, use delete for gas refunds and events for off-chain data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: State cleanup
keyIdea.text: Delete unused storage to earn refunds and emit events for off-chain needs rather than storing everything on-chain.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › delete & emit
Gas refunds

Deleting a storage variable sets it to zero and produces a gas refund as an incentive to reduce state. Use it when the data is truly obsolete.

Events vs Storage
Emitting events stores data in logs which is cheaper than sstore. Use events for UI updates or indexing, not for persistent on-chain logic.
Cautions
  • Do not delete state merely to capture refunds without clear semantic reason.
  • Events are not accessible to on-chain contracts; they are off-chain signals.
  • Measure the net gas impact of deletes and new writes before refactoring.

screens.title: Hands-on Refactor: GasInefficient → GasEfficient
screens.subtitle: Refactor patterns: packing, caching, visibility, and delete

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete refactor using the provided GasInefficient starter contract. The refactor goals are explicit: use smaller packed types for sets of small variables, cache storage reads in loops, change where functions accept arrays to external with calldata, and use delete where state truly becomes obsolete. For packing, replace three uint256 state variables that represent small flags or counters with uint8 and bool and place them consecutively so the compiler can pack them. For loops, cache myNumbers. length into a local uint256 and load items into memory within the loop to avoid repeated sloads. For visibility, change addNumber to external if it only receives one uint256 parameter from external callers, avoiding unnecessary copying. Finally, when removing elements from arrays that are no longer needed, use delete to free slots and receive a gas refund. After implementing these changes in GasEfficient, deploy both contracts on a local Hardhat network and compare gasUsed for addNumber, sumNumbers, and setBalance with hardhat-gas-reporter or Remix's profiler. The test confirms whether real savings exist. Which refactor do you expect to yield the largest gas decrease in your contract?

keyIdea.title: Refactor steps
keyIdea.text: Apply packing, cached reads, external visibility where appropriate, and delete for cleanup; measure before and after with a gas reporter.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Hands-on Refactor
Starter code (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract GasInefficient {
  uint256[] public myNumbers;
  mapping(address => uint256) public balances;
  address public owner;

  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }

  function addNumber(uint256 _num) public { myNumbers.push(_num); }

  function sumNumbers() public view returns (uint256) {
    uint256 total = 0;
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < myNumbers.length; i++) {
      total += myNumbers[i];
    }
    return total;
  }

  function setBalance(address _user, uint256 _amount) public { require(msg.sender == owner, "Not authorized"); balances[_user] = _amount; }
}
Refactored snippets
// Packed state variables
uint8 public smallA;
uint8 public smallB;
bool public flag;
uint256 public bigValue;

// Cached loop + memory access
function sumNumbers() public view returns (uint256) {
  uint256 total = 0;
  uint256 len = myNumbers.length;
  for (uint256 i = 0; i < len; i++) {
    uint256 value = myNumbers[i];
    total += value;
  }
  return total;
}

// External signature avoids copying for arrays
function addNumber(uint256 _num) external { myNumbers.push(_num); }

// Use delete when appropriate
function removeNumber(uint256 i) external { delete myNumbers[i]; }

screens.title: Measuring Gas: Tools and Workflow
screens.subtitle: Use Hardhat, gas reporters, or Remix to verify savings

narration.text: Measuring is the guardrail that prevents wasted effort. The chapter recommends using Hardhat's hardhat-gas-reporter or Remix's gas profiler to quantify gasUsed for specific function calls and transactions. Your workflow should be: deploy a baseline contract, run representative transactions to collect gasUsed, implement a single targeted refactor, and then rerun the same transactions to compare results. Keep changes small and isolated so you can attribute improvements to a single modification. Reporting tools will show gasUsed per call and allow you to compare totals. A common pitfall is relying on a single measurement; run several transactions and average results to account for any variability. Also, ensure functional tests accompany gas measurements to confirm behavior remains correct. Finally, document your findings: a table or short report that includes baseline gasUsed, refactored gasUsed, and percentage change will make it easy to review and share results with your team. narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to keep at hand. First, gas measures EVM work; reducing gasUsed lowers user fees. Second, gasPrice multiplies gasUsed to produce transaction cost; while price varies, your code controls gasUsed. Third, gasUsed is what you can optimize through data layout, algorithm choices, and visibility. Use these three as the baseline for decisions. When you design contracts, favor memory for temporary work, group small state variables to allow packing, and avoid unbounded storage loops. Gas
Unit of computational effort used by the EVM and paid in Ether.
Gas Price
Amount of Ether paid per gas unit; set by users and network demand.
Gas Used
Total gas consumed by a transaction; it's the main lever developers can optimize.
Summary
When optimizing, reduce storage writes, prefer memory for temporary data, pack small variables, cache reads in loops, choose external for array inputs, and measure with a gas reporter.

narration.text: These quick reference cards are meant for code reviews and pull requests. First: Storage vs Memory — prefer memory or calldata for temporary or externally passed data. Second: Data Packing — group small variables consecutively so the compiler packs them into fewer slots. Third: Short-circuiting & Visibility — order cheap checks first and use external to avoid memory copies for arrays. Use these three checks as a fast review checklist when you open a Solidity file. Finally, always pair changes with gas measurements so you can justify the added complexity, if any.
